passed.title: pl.concat_str returns null for the whole row if any input is null
passed.trap: By default `pl.concat_str` uses `ignore_nulls=False`, so a single null in any input column makes the entire concatenated string null. This is not how Python string joining behaves. Pass `ignore_nulls=True` to skip null parts.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"first": ["Ann", "Bob"], "middle": [None, "J"], "last": ["Lee", "Kim"]})
out = df.select(
    default=pl.concat_str("first", "middle", "last", separator=" "),
    skip_nulls=pl.concat_str("first", "middle", "last", separator=" ", ignore_nulls=True),
)
print(out["default"].to_list())
print(out["skip_nulls"].to_list())

passed.title: pl.count counts non-null values, not rows; use pl.len for row counts
passed.trap: `pl.count("a")` is sugar for `pl.col("a").count()` and returns the number of **non-null** values, not the number of rows. Calling `pl.count()` with no arguments to get a row count is deprecated. Use `pl.len()` when you mean the number of rows, the equivalent of SQL `COUNT(*)`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3]})
out = df.select(non_null=pl.count("a"), rows=pl.len())
print(out.columns, out.rows())

passed.title: pl.all with column names aggregates instead of selecting, and skips nulls by default
passed.trap: `pl.all()` with no arguments selects every column. `pl.all("a")` does **not** select column `a`. It is sugar for `pl.col("a").all()` and collapses the column to a single boolean. `pl.all` and `pl.any` also default to `ignore_nulls=True`, so an all-null column gives `True` for `pl.all` and `False` for `pl.any`. To select a column use `pl.col`, and pass `ignore_nulls=False` to get Kleene (null-propagating) logic.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"a": [True, None], "b": [None, None]},
    schema={"a": pl.Boolean, "b": pl.Boolean},
)
print(df.select(pl.all()).shape)  # all columns, 2 rows
print(df.select(pl.all("a")).shape)  # aggregated, 1 row
print(df.select(pl.all("b")).item())  # all-null column -> True
print(df.select(pl.any("b")).item())  # all-null column -> False
print(df.select(pl.all("a", "b", ignore_nulls=False)).rows())  # Kleene -> None

passed.title: Null results from pl.all_horizontal/pl.any_horizontal make rows vanish from filters
passed.trap: `pl.all_horizontal` and `pl.any_horizontal` use Kleene logic, so a row whose result is undetermined (`True AND null`, `False OR null`) becomes null rather than `False`. A filter drops null rows, and negating null is still null. Such rows therefore disappear from both `DataFrame.filter(cond)` and `DataFrame.filter(~cond)`. Call `Expr.fill_null(False)` (or `True`) on the condition if every row must land on one side.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "x": [True, True, False], "y": [True, None, True]})
cond = pl.all_horizontal("x", "y")
print(df.select(cond).to_series().to_list())
print(df.filter(cond).height, df.filter(~cond).height)  # 1 + 1, row 2 lost
safe = cond.fill_null(False)
print(df.filter(safe).height, df.filter(~safe).height)  # 1 + 2

passed.title: pl.coalesce skips nulls but keeps NaN, and literals can change the dtype
passed.trap: `pl.coalesce` keeps the first **non-null** value. In Polars, `NaN` is a valid float value, not a missing one, so a `NaN` wins over a later fallback. Convert NaN to null first with `Expr.fill_nan(None)`. Also, the output dtype is the supertype of all inputs, so a float fallback literal such as `0.0` turns an integer column into `Float64`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [float("nan"), None, 1.0], "b": [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]})
out = df.with_columns(
    naive=pl.coalesce("a", "b"),
    fixed=pl.coalesce(pl.col("a").fill_nan(None), "b"),
)
print(out["naive"].to_list())
print(out["fixed"].to_list())
ints = pl.DataFrame({"i": [None, 2]})
print(ints.select(pl.coalesce("i", 0.0)).dtypes)

passed.title: Range functions return expressions by default, and endpoint inclusion differs
passed.trap: `pl.arange` and `pl.date_range` return an `Expr` unless you pass `eager=True`, so code expecting a `Series` gets an expression instead. Endpoints are also inconsistent between them. `pl.arange` (an alias of `pl.int_range`) excludes `end`. `pl.date_range` and `pl.date_ranges` default to `closed="both"` and include `end`; pass `closed="left"` for a half-open date range.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import date

print(isinstance(pl.arange(0, 3), pl.Expr))  # True: Expr, not Series
print(pl.arange(0, 3, eager=True).to_list())  # end excluded
print(pl.date_range(date(2024, 1, 1), date(2024, 1, 3), eager=True).to_list())  # end included
print(
    pl.date_range(date(2024, 1, 1), date(2024, 1, 3), closed="left", eager=True).to_list()
)

passed.title: pl.concat defaults to strict vertical stacking with no column alignment or type coercion
passed.trap: With the default `how="vertical"`, `pl.concat` needs the frames to have the same columns with the same dtypes. It does not fill missing columns with nulls or upcast mismatched types; it raises instead. Use `how="vertical_relaxed"` to coerce to a common supertype. Use `how="diagonal"` (or `"diagonal_relaxed"`) to take the union of columns and fill the gaps with null.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

a = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2]})
b = pl.DataFrame({"x": [0.5]})
c = pl.DataFrame({"x": [3], "y": ["new"]})
for other in (b, c):
    try:
        pl.concat([a, other])
        print("no error")
    except Exception as e:
        print(type(e))
relaxed = pl.concat([a, b], how="vertical_relaxed")
print(relaxed.schema, relaxed.rows())
diag = pl.concat([a, c], how="diagonal")
print(diag.columns, diag.rows())

passed.title: pl.business_day_count excludes the end date and is unstable
passed.trap: `pl.business_day_count` counts business days from `start` up to but **not including** `end`, so a Monday-to-Friday span returns 4, not 5. To count inclusively, shift `end` forward by one day, for example with `Expr.dt.offset_by`. Dates listed in `holidays` are also excluded from the count. The function is marked unstable and may change without notice.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import date

df = pl.DataFrame({"start": [date(2024, 1, 1)], "end": [date(2024, 1, 5)]})  # Mon..Fri
out = df.select(
    exclusive=pl.business_day_count("start", "end"),
    inclusive=pl.business_day_count("start", pl.col("end").dt.offset_by("1d")),
    with_holiday=pl.business_day_count("start", "end", holidays=[date(2024, 1, 2)]),
)
print(out.columns, out.rows())
